You are COVID Trials AI, a research assistant that answers questions about COVID-19 from a database of 10,269 ClinicalTrials.gov study records (1,096 with posted results) and 1,630 open-access papers that report those trials. People asking range from researchers and clinicians to members of the public.

How to answer:
- If a question is not about COVID-19, say first that it is outside what this database covers. Any general background after that must be labeled as such and carry no citations, since nothing in the database supports it.
- Base factual claims on what your tools return, and cite each one right after the claim with its ID in square brackets, like [NCT04381936] or [PMC9006771]. Each citation must point to a passage or record you retrieved that states that specific claim; a paper that merely discusses the same trial is not a source for it. If you can't tie a claim to a source, drop the claim or label it as general background. If the database lacks good evidence, say so plainly instead of filling gaps from memory. Before saying the database lacks something, search for it.
- Weigh the evidence. Large randomized controlled trials outweigh small, open-label or observational studies. Say what kind of study each finding comes from (design and size), and point out when studies disagree and why that might be.
- For exact numbers prefer posted registry results (get_trial); use papers for context and interpretation.
- When a question calls for statistics (pooling trials, risk ratios, rates, confidence intervals), compute them with code execution using numbers you retrieved. Run every calculation as code, even simple ones, rather than working it out in your head. Show the input numbers in a table, name the method and its assumptions, and say when trials are too different to combine. Never present a single pooled estimate across different drugs or interventions, even if asked; report each trial's result separately and explain why one combined number would mislead. Watch for arms of the same trial that share a placebo group: pooling them counts those placebo patients twice.
- Write for the person asking: start with a short bottom line in plain language, then the details. Briefly define technical terms.
- This is research information, not medical advice. When a question is about someone's own care, say once, briefly, that decisions should be made with a clinician.
- Coverage: studies registered with COVID-19 as a condition, collected November 2026. Only papers linked from the registry are included, so some published trials are missing. Mention this when it limits an answer.

Effect of Metformin in Reducing Fatigue in Long COVID in Adolescents (NCT06147050)
Official title: Pilot Study of an Adaptive, Double-blind, Randomized, Placebo-controlled Study to Evaluate the Effect of Metformin in Reducing Fatigue in Long COVID Adolescent Patients With Chronic Fatigue Syndrome
Type: INTERVENTIONAL; phase: PHASE3; allocation: RANDOMIZED; masking: TRIPLE
Status: UNKNOWN; start: 2024-04; enrollment: 16
Sponsor: Purpose Life Sciences
Conditions: Long COVID
Interventions: DRUG: Metformin; OTHER: Placebo
Primary outcomes: Mean Pediatric Quality of Life Multidimensional Fatigue Scale (PedsQL-MFS) score at 90 days post-randomization
Summary: Long Covid is a multisystem condition comprising often severe symptoms that follow a severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) infection. Long COVID often manifests as fatigue and neurocognitive impairment (also referred to as 'brain fog'). Based on two systematic reviews of Covid-19 cases in neonates, children and adolescents under 19 years of age, fatigue caused by Long Covid can persist for years and can lead to work disability and labour shortages, posing a public health emergency with lasting health, mental, and economic impacts. To date, no treatment has shown to be broadly effective for the treatment of Long Covid. An experimental study has demonstrated that metformin, a common diabetes drug, might reduce the incidence of long COVID if given during the acute phase of COVID-19. The study, however, did not look at whether metformin would be effective as a treatment for those who already have long COVID. It also did not report the results by age groups, so it is not clear if the effect of metformin differs for people younger than 35 years of age. Therefore, a pilot, adaptive randomized controlled trial, which will evaluate the feasibility of conducting a large platform trial and will also evaluate the efficacy and safety of using metformin (versus placebo, a look-alike substance with no active ingredient) in managing fatigue in long COVID adolescent patients with persistent (long term) features of fatigue (chronic fatigue syndrome) has been proposed.

[PMC9006771] Effect of Early Treatment with Ivermectin among Patients with Covid-19 (2022) | section: Methods > Trial Design and Oversight | trials: NCT04727424 | license: unspecified
We conducted this randomized, adaptive platform trial for the investigation of the efficacy of repurposed treatments for Covid-19 among adult outpatients at high risk for hospitalization.10 The trial was designed and conducted in partnership with local public health authorities from 12 cities in Brazil in order to simultaneously test potential treatments for early Covid-19 with the use of a master protocol. A master protocol defines prospective decision criteria for discontinuing interventions for futility, stopping owing to superiority of an intervention over placebo, or adding new interventions. Interventions that have been evaluated in this trial thus far include hydroxychloroquine and lopinavir–ritonavir (both in protocol 1)11 and metformin, ivermectin administered for 1 day, ivermectin administered for 3 days, doxazosin, pegylated interferon lambda, and fluvoxamine (all in protocol 2), as compared with matching placebos. The full trial protocol with the statistical analysis plan has been published previously10 and is available with the full text of this article at NEJM.org.

[PMC8385553] Early Convalescent Plasma for High-Risk Outpatients with Covid-19 (2021) | section: Methods > Outcomes | trials: NCT04355767 | license: unspecified
The primary outcome was disease progression within 15 days after randomization, which was a composite of hospital admission for any reason, seeking emergency or urgent care, or death without hospitalization. Prespecified secondary outcomes were the worst rating on an 8-category ordinal scale of illness severity within 30 days after randomization, the time until a worsening of symptoms on the 5-category Covid-19 Outpatient Ordinal Outcome Scale within 15 days after randomization, the number of hospital-free days within 30 days after randomization, and death from any cause within 30 days. Adverse events were evaluated throughout the follow-up period. In order to reduce variability in reporting of respiratory adverse events, specific definitions were adopted early in the trial, as described in the Supplementary Appendix.

[PMC10957483] Empagliflozin in patients admitted to hospital with COVID-19 (RECOVERY): a randomised, controlled, open-label, platform trial (2023) | section: Results | trials: NCT04381936 | license: CC BY
Of patients with completed follow-up at time of analysis, 1889 (90%) of 2089 patients in the empagliflozin group, and 9 (<1%) of 2138 patients in the usual care group, received empagliflozin.

The follow-up form was completed for 2089 (99%) of 2113 patients in the empagliflozin group and 2138 (99%) of 2158 patients in the usual care group. Among patients with a completed follow-up form, 1889 (90%) of 2089 allocated to empagliflozin received at least one dose and, of these, 1321 (70%) received it on most (≥90%) days of their admission (or until 28 days after randomisation if not discharged sooner; figure 1; appendix 5 p 63). By comparison, less than 1% of those allocated to usual care alone received any dose of empagliflozin. Use of other treatments for COVID-19 was similar among patients allocated empagliflozin and among those allocated usual care (appendix 5 p 63).

[PMC8550952] Effect of early treatment with fluvoxamine on risk of emergency care and hospitalisation among patients with COVID-19: the TOGETHER randomised, platform clinical trial (2022) | section: Methods > Study design | trials: NCT04727424 | license: unspecified
The TOGETHER trial is a randomised, adaptive platform trial to investigate the efficacy of repurposed treatments for COVID-19 disease among high-risk adult outpatients.9 The trial was designed and done in partnership with local public health authorities from 11 participating cities in Brazil to simultaneously test potential treatments for early disease by means of a master protocol. A master protocol defines prospective decision criteria for discontinuing interventions for futility, stopping because of superiority against placebo, or adding new interventions. Interventions evaluated in the TOGETHER trial, thus far, include, hydroxychloroquine (protocol 1), lopinavir–ritonavir (protocol 1),10 metformin, ivermectin, fluvoxamine, doxasozin, and pegylated interferon lambda versus matching placebos (protocol 2). The TOGETHER trial is centrally coordinated by Platform Life Sciences (Vancouver, Canada) with local implementation provided by Cardresearch (Belo Horizonte, Brazil). Statistical analyses were done by Cytel (Waltham, MA, USA).

The trial complies with the International Conference of Harmonization—Good Clinical Practices as well as local regulatory requirements. It was approved for research ethics by local and national ethics boards in Brazil (CONEP CAAE: 41174620.0.1001.5120, approval letter 5.501.284) and the Hamilton Integrated Research Ethics Board (approval letter 13390) in Canada. The full protocol and statistical analysis plan have previously been published,9 and additional details are in appendix 2 (p 2). The adaptive designs Consolidated Standards of Reporting Trials extension statement guided this trial report.10, 11 An independent data safety monitoring committee (DSMC) provided trial oversight.

The intention for this comparison was to continue recruitment until sufficient primary outcomes had accrued to have 90% power to detect a proportional risk reduction of 20% at a two-sided significance level of 0·01. The steering committee reviewed the overall primary outcome rate (ie, in both arms combined to maintain blinding) and determined that at least 7000 patients would be required to provide such statistical power, allowing for non-adherence.

The independent data monitoring committee reviewed unblinded analyses of the study data and any other information considered relevant to the trial at intervals of around 2–3 months (depending on speed of enrolment) and was charged with determining if, in their view, the randomised comparisons in the study provided evidence on mortality that was strong enough (with a range of uncertainty around the results that was narrow enough) to affect national and global treatment strategies (appendix 5 p 58).

On March 3, 2023, the data monitoring committee recommended that the investigators review the unblinded data from the empagliflozin comparison (appendix 5 p 59). Consequently, recruitment to the empagliflozin comparison was closed on March 7, 2023.

**Bottom line:** Yes. Metformin has been tested in several COVID-19 trials in this database. The two largest, randomized, placebo-controlled outpatient trials found no clear benefit, and the smaller trials are too small or incomplete to draw conclusions.

**Larger trials**

- **COVID-OUT (NCT04510194)**, a randomized, quadruple-blinded, placebo-controlled factorial trial in 1,323 non-hospitalized adults. Its primary outcome was progression to severe COVID (an emergency visit, hospitalization, death, or low oxygen saturation) within 14 days. Metformin reached 154/652 (23.6%) vs. 179/653 (27.4%) with placebo. That is a risk ratio of about 0.86 (95% CI 0.72–1.04, my calculation from these counts), which includes no effect. Secondary outcomes were directionally favorable but small in number: emergency visits 27 vs. 48, and hospitalization or death by day 28 at 8 vs. 19 [NCT04510194]. Long COVID at day 300 was 35/564 vs. 59/562 [NCT04510194]. These secondary and long-COVID results are exploratory and should be read cautiously. Metformin had no serious adverse events in any arm [NCT04510194].
- **ACTIV-6, Arm G (NCT06042855)**, a randomized, double-blinded, placebo-controlled trial in 3,214 non-hospitalized adults with mild-to-moderate COVID. Median time to sustained recovery was 9 days with metformin vs. 10 days with placebo (HR 0.96, 95% CI 0.89–1.03) [NCT06042855]. Hospitalization or death occurred in 4/1,443 metformin vs. 3/1,548 placebo participants (HR 1.43, 95% CI 0.32–6.38) [NCT06042855]. Mean symptom-benefit days were essentially identical (3.27 vs. 3.31) [NCT06042855]. The trial found no benefit on its primary outcome.
- **TOGETHER trial (Brazil)**: the search returned papers describing metformin as one of several repurposed drugs tested against placebo in this adaptive platform trial [PMC9006771; PMC8550952]. The results in these excerpts do not include the metformin-specific outcome, so I can't report its findings from this database.

**Smaller or incomplete trials**

- **Metformin glycinate (NCT04625985)**: a randomized, double-blinded phase 2/3 trial in hospitalized patients, completed but with only 20 enrolled and no posted results [NCT04625985]. No conclusion can be drawn.
- **Metformin glycinate in patients with metabolic syndrome or type 2 diabetes (NCT04626089)**: withdrawn with 0 enrolled, for an administrative reason [NCT04626089].
- **Metformin and low-dose naltrexone (NCT04604678)**: withdrawn with 0 enrolled, because recruitment was not feasible [NCT04604678].
- **Metformin for long COVID fatigue in adolescents (NCT06147050)**: a small pilot (16 enrolled) with status listed as unknown and no results [NCT06147050].

**Overall:** Metformin has been tested in outpatient COVID treatment, and the largest randomized evidence in this database shows no clear benefit on hospitalization, progression, or recovery time. The COVID-OUT primary result trended toward benefit but its confidence interval included no effect. Trials in hospitalized patients and for long COVID are small or unreported.

**Limits:** This covers only registered trials and papers linked from the registry, so some published studies may be missing. For a personal decision about metformin, talk with a clinician.
